accessibility: Designing a system so that people of all abilities, including those with disabilities, can use it equally.
application software: Programs that run on top of the operating system to perform specific tasks for a user, such as a browser or word processor.
cache memory: A small, very fast memory close to the CPU that stores frequently used data to reduce access delays.
central processing unit, cpu: The hardware that interprets and executes program instructions, containing the control unit, ALU, and registers.
change management: The process of managing the organisational and human changes that come with introducing a new system.
data migration: The process of transferring data from an old system to a new one, including conversion and integrity checks.
device driver: Software that lets the operating system communicate with and control a specific hardware device.
direct changeover / big-bang: A strategy that stops the old system entirely and switches to the new one all at once.
error prevention: A design principle that minimises mistakes through input validation, confirmations, and undo features.
fetch-decode-execute cycle: The basic CPU cycle of fetching an instruction, decoding it, and executing it, repeated continuously.
human-computer interaction, hci: The study and design of how people interact with computer systems and interfaces.
ip address: A logical address that identifies a device on an IP network, used for routing data to it.
legacy system: An older system still in use for key tasks but difficult to integrate with modern technology.
local area network: A network covering a small area such as one building, owned and managed by a single organisation.
media access control address: A permanent 48-bit hardware identifier assigned to a network interface card, used at the data link layer.
network topology: The physical or logical arrangement in which devices are connected in a network, such as bus, star, or mesh.
operating system, os: System software that manages hardware resources and provides an interface for applications to use them.
packet switching: Sending data as small packets routed independently and reassembled at the destination.
parallel running: A changeover strategy that runs the old and new systems together for a time to compare results.
phased implementation: Introducing the new system's features in stages, stabilising each before moving on.
pilot changeover: Trialling the new system in one part of an organisation before rolling it out everywhere.
process scheduling: The OS mechanism that decides how multiple processes share CPU time.
program counter, pc: A register that holds the memory address of the next instruction to be executed.
protocol: A set of rules and standards defining how data is exchanged over a network.
random access memory: Volatile main memory that temporarily holds the programs and data the CPU is currently using.
read-only memory: Non-volatile memory whose contents can only be read, typically storing the boot firmware.
requirements analysis: The stage of identifying and documenting what a new system must do.
secondary storage: Non-volatile storage that holds large amounts of data permanently, such as a hard drive or SSD.
stakeholder: Anyone with an interest in a system's development or use, such as users, managers, or customers.
star topology: A layout where every device connects to a central hub or switch, which is a single point of failure.
system development life cycle, sdlc: A framework defining the stages of planning, building, and maintaining an information system.
usability: How effectively, efficiently, and satisfyingly users can achieve their goals with a system.
user acceptance testing, uat: Testing by end users in realistic conditions to confirm the system meets their requirements.
user resistance: The tendency of staff to reject a new system or cling to old ways of working.
volatile memory: Memory that loses its stored data when power is removed, such as RAM.
wide area network: A network spanning a large geographic area, typically leasing infrastructure from telecom providers.
american standard code for information i: A character encoding standard that maps text characters to fixed 7-bit (or 8-bit) integer codes.
arithmetic logic unit, alu: The CPU circuit that performs arithmetic and logical operations on data from registers.
binary / base-2: A number system using only the digits 0 and 1, matching the on/off states of computer circuits.
bit·byte: A bit is a single 0 or 1; eight bits make one byte, the basic unit for measuring data.
boolean algebra: A system of logic using true and false values with AND, OR, and NOT operations to simplify expressions.
bus width: The number of bits that can be transferred at once between the CPU and memory or devices.
cache hit rate: The proportion of times the CPU finds the data it needs in the cache rather than in RAM.
character encoding: A standard that maps characters to integer codes, such as ASCII or Unicode.
clock speed: The number of cycles a CPU performs per second, measured in hertz.
combinational logic circuit: A digital circuit whose output depends only on its current inputs, not on any stored state.
control unit, cu: The CPU part that interprets instructions and directs the other components in the correct order.
de morgan's laws: Rules stating NOT(A AND B) = NOT A OR NOT B, and NOT(A OR B) = NOT A AND NOT B.
hexadecimal / base-16: A number system using digits 0–9 and A–F, where each digit represents four binary bits.
functional completeness: The property of a gate set that can build every possible Boolean function, as NAND or NOR alone can.
memory address register, mar: A register that holds the address of the memory cell the CPU will read from or write to.
memory data register, mdr: A register that temporarily holds data being read from or written to memory.
memory hierarchy: The layered arrangement of storage from fast, small registers down to large, slow secondary storage.
multi-core: A CPU design with two or more independent cores on one chip that can process instructions in parallel.
truth table: A table listing the output of a logic function for every possible combination of its inputs.
two's complement: A method of representing negative numbers by inverting all bits of the positive value and adding one.
배타적 or, exclusive or: A logic gate whose output is 1 only when its two inputs differ.
인버터, inverter: A single-input gate (the NOT gate) that outputs the opposite of its input.
asymmetric encryption / public-key encry: Encryption that uses a public key to encrypt and a separate private key to decrypt, as in RSA.
bandwidth: The maximum amount of data a network link can transmit per unit of time.
client-server model: A network architecture where clients request services from dedicated, centrally managed servers.
domain name system, dns: A distributed system that translates human-readable domain names into IP addresses.
firewall: A security system that allows or blocks network traffic according to predefined rules.
hypertext transfer protocol, http/https: An application-layer protocol for exchanging web data; HTTPS adds TLS encryption.
internet protocol address: A logical network-layer address that identifies a device's location for routing packets.
interoperability: The ability of different systems and devices to communicate and exchange data via common standards.
local area network, lan: A network over a limited area, owned by one organisation, with high bandwidth and low latency.
lossless compression: Compression that reduces file size while allowing the original data to be restored exactly.
lossy compression: Compression that removes hard-to-notice information to shrink files, so the original cannot be fully restored.
malware: Malicious software designed to harm or infiltrate a system, such as viruses, worms, or ransomware.
open systems interconnection model: A reference model dividing network communication into seven layers, from physical to application.
peer-to-peer model, p2p: An architecture where each device acts as both client and server, sharing resources without a central server.
personal area network, pan: A small network connecting personal devices within a few metres, often using Bluetooth or NFC.
run-length encoding, rle: A lossless technique that replaces runs of repeated values with a value-and-count pair.
single point of failure, spof: A component whose failure stops the entire system, such as a central server or hub.
standard: A technical specification set by a standards body so devices from different makers can work together.
symmetric encryption: Encryption that uses the same secret key to both encrypt and decrypt, as in AES.
transmission control protocol, tcp: A transport-layer protocol providing reliable, connection-oriented communication with ordering and retransmission.
user datagram protocol, udp: A connectionless transport-layer protocol with low overhead and no guarantee of delivery or order.
virtual private network, vpn: A technology creating an encrypted tunnel over the public internet for secure private communication.
wide area network, wan: A network spanning large geographic areas, such as the internet, usually owned by service providers.
abstraction: Removing unnecessary detail to keep only the essential features of a problem.
algorithm efficiency: How much resource, such as time or memory, an algorithm uses to solve a problem of a given size.
binary search: Searching a sorted array by repeatedly comparing the middle element and halving the search range.
bubble sort: A sort that repeatedly compares adjacent elements and swaps them if they are in the wrong order.
decomposition: Breaking a complex problem into smaller, manageable sub-problems that can be solved separately.
flowchart: A diagram that uses standard shapes and arrows to represent the logical flow of an algorithm.
iteration / loop: A control structure that repeats a block of instructions while a condition holds or for a set count.
linear search: Searching by comparing each element in turn from the start until the target is found.
mid index: The index of the middle position of the current search range in a binary search, mid = (low + high) DIV 2.
pass: One complete sweep through the array in a sorting algorithm.
postcondition: A condition that must be true after an algorithm or function has finished executing correctly.
precondition: A condition that must be true before an algorithm or function runs in order for it to work correctly.
pseudocode: A way of expressing an algorithm's logic between natural language and a programming language, without specific syntax.
selection / branching: A control structure that chooses between blocks of instructions based on whether a condition is true.
selection sort: A sort that repeatedly finds the smallest unsorted element and places it at the front of the unsorted part.
swap: An operation that exchanges the values of two variables, usually using a temporary variable.
thinking ahead: Anticipating preconditions, valid inputs, and possible exceptions before designing an algorithm.
thinking concurrently: Approaching a problem by splitting it into independent parts that can run at the same time.
thinking logically: Evaluating conditions to choose between different execution paths within an algorithm.
thinking procedurally: Breaking a problem into ordered steps to be carried out in sequence.
trace table: A table that records how each variable's value changes as an algorithm executes step by step.
base case: The condition in a recursive function that returns a result directly without calling itself again.
binary tree terminology: The naming of tree parts such as root, leaf, internal node, level, height, and subtree.
call stack: The stack-structured memory region that stores local variables, parameters, and return addresses for function calls.
circular linked list: A linked list whose last node points back to the first node, allowing endless traversal.
divide and conquer: Splitting a problem into independent sub-problems, solving each recursively, and combining the results.
doubly linked list: A linked list where each node holds pointers to both the next and the previous node.
dynamic data structure: A data structure whose size can change at run time as needed, such as a linked list or tree.
inorder traversal: Visiting a binary tree as left subtree, root, then right subtree.
insertion in singly linked list: Adding a new node by first pointing it to the next node, then updating the previous node's pointer to it.
iterative approach: Solving a problem using loops, which keeps memory use constant compared with recursion.
overflow / underflow: Overflow is adding to a full stack or queue; underflow is removing from an empty one.
pointer: A variable that stores the memory address of another piece of data, such as a node.
postorder traversal: Visiting a binary tree as left subtree, right subtree, then root.
preorder traversal: Visiting a binary tree as root, left subtree, then right subtree.
queue: A first-in-first-out data structure where the earliest added element is the first removed.
recursive case: The part of a recursive function that calls itself on a smaller sub-problem, moving toward the base case.
singly linked list: A basic linked list where each node holds data and a single pointer to the next node.
stack: A last-in-first-out data structure where the most recently added element is the first removed.
stack overflow: A runtime error that occurs when recursion grows too deep for the call stack to hold more frames.
static data structure: A data structure whose size is fixed before run time and cannot change, such as an array.
tail recursion: Recursion where the recursive call is the function's last operation, allowing optimisation into a loop.
two-dimensional array: An array arranged in rows and columns, accessed with two indices such as A[row][col].
context switch: The process by which the OS saves one process's state and loads another's to run on the CPU.
fragmentation: The scattering of free memory into small pieces as blocks are repeatedly allocated and freed.
interrupt: A signal telling the CPU to stop its current task and handle an event, such as a timer interrupt.
lru: least recently used: A page-replacement algorithm that evicts the page that has gone unused for the longest time.
memory management: The OS functions that allocate and free RAM among processes and prevent them from interfering.
memory protection: An OS and hardware mechanism ensuring each process can only access its own allocated memory.
multitasking: An OS feature that rapidly switches between processes so users seem to run several tasks at once.
page and page frame: A page is a fixed-size block of virtual memory; a page frame is the matching block of physical RAM.
page fault: An interrupt that occurs when a process accesses a page not currently loaded in RAM.
page table: An OS data structure mapping a process's virtual page numbers to physical frame numbers.
peripherals: Input and output devices connected to a computer besides the CPU and main memory.
primary memory / ram: Fast, volatile memory the CPU accesses directly to hold currently running programs and data.
processor speed: The CPU's computing capacity, expressed as instructions per second or clock frequency in GHz.
round-robin scheduling: A scheduling algorithm that gives each process a fixed time slice in turn.
shared vs dedicated resources: Shared resources are time-sliced among processes, while dedicated resources are used exclusively by one at a time.
swapping: Moving pages or whole processes between RAM and disk storage to manage limited memory.
thrashing: A state where the system spends more time swapping pages than doing useful work.
virtual memory: A technique giving each process its own address space independent of the actual amount of RAM.
working set: The set of pages a process is actively using within a given time window.
actuator: An output device that converts a controller's command into a physical action such as motion or heat.
automatic door / washing machine / eleva: Common control systems where sensors feed a controller that drives actuators like motors and valves.
autonomous agent: A system that independently perceives its environment and decides actions to achieve a goal without direct control.
centralised control: A control structure where one central controller processes all inputs and commands all actuators.
closed-loop control: Control that feeds the measured output back to the controller to correct error against a setpoint.
distributed control: A structure where several independent controllers manage their own areas and communicate to cooperate.
ipo: input-process-output cycle: The basic control flow of taking input from sensors, processing it, and producing output to actuators.
lag / delay: The time it takes for an input change to be reflected in a control system's output.
microprocessor / controller: The 'brain' of a control system that processes sensor input and issues commands to actuators.
negative feedback: Feedback that reduces action when output exceeds the setpoint and increases it when below, driving error to zero.
open-loop control: Control that sends preset commands without checking the actual output against a setpoint.
overcorrection and overshoot: When a controller corrects too far and passes the setpoint, causing oscillation around it.
sensor: An input device that detects a physical change in the environment and converts it into an electrical signal.
setpoint and error: The setpoint is the target value, and error is the difference between the setpoint and the current value.
thermostat / central heating: A closed-loop system where a temperature sensor's feedback controls a heater to maintain a setpoint.
traffic light control: A control system that sequences traffic signals, either on a fixed timer or dynamically from sensor data.
transducer: A device that converts one form of energy into another, such as an ADC or DAC in a control system.
아날로그-디지털 변환기 / analogue-to-digital conve: A circuit that samples an analogue sensor signal and encodes each measurement as a binary number.
